chunks: "I'll walk through it from the microcontroller to the gate. On the input side the LED needs about 10 milliamps to get good CTR and speed. A 3. 3 volt GPIO, an LED drop of about 1.
2 volts, so the resistor is 2. 1 volts over 10 milliamps, 210 ohms, and I'd use 200. I drive it active-high so that when the pin is low or floating, the LED is off.
On the output side the phototransistor sits on an isolated 12 volt supply. If I just put a pull-up on the collector and wire that to the gate, two things go wrong.
First, the output is inverted, so a high at the microcontroller would give a low at the gate, and the default at reset would turn the FET on.
Second, a pull-up of several kilohms into a gate capacitance of a nanofarad or two gives a time constant of microseconds, which is far too slow.
So I use the phototransistor as an emitter follower: collector to the 12 volts, emitter to a pulldown of 6. 8 kilohms, and I take the voltage across that resistor.
With the LED on, the phototransistor passes at least 2 milliamps at end of life, so that node goes to about 11 volts, and with the LED off it's pulled to ground.
That's non-inverting and defaults to off.
That node is high impedance, so I follow it with an NPN and PNP emitter-follower pair that supplies and sinks the gate current, with a 10 ohm gate resistor and a 100 k gate-source pulldown.
Then I check the numbers at worst case: CTR at end of life and hot, the delays on a scope, and that the barrier's CMTI is higher than my dv/dt."
